scenes.visual: Title card: One Border, Many Destinations.

scenes.tts: Hearing loss, a white forelock, and a stretch of gut with no nerve cells. Why would one gene cause all three?
scenes.visual: A child's face with a white forelock; beside it a gut diagram with the far end greyed out. Three question marks.
scenes.narration: Hearing loss, a white forelock, and a stretch of gut with no nerve cells. Why would one gene cause all three?

scenes.tts: Some patients have Hirschsprung disease and Waardenburg syndrome together, from one mutant gene. Hold that puzzle.
scenes.visual: Labels appear under the images: Hirschsprung disease (gut), Waardenburg syndrome (pigment, hearing). A single gene icon links them.
scenes.narration: Some patients have Hirschsprung disease and Waardenburg syndrome together, from one mutant gene. Hold that puzzle.

scenes.tts: Early on, the ectoderm splits into neural plate and future skin. The neural crest forms at the border between them.
scenes.visual: A flat sheet: slate neural plate in the middle, pale future skin at the sides, a gold band at each edge labelled neural crest.
scenes.narration: Early on, the ectoderm splits into neural plate and future skin. The neural crest forms at the border between them.

scenes.tts: When the plate rolls up into the neural tube, the border cells end up along its top.
scenes.visual: The sheet folds into a tube; the two gold bands meet along the dorsal midline.
scenes.narration: When the plate rolls up into the neural tube, the border cells end up along its top.

scenes.tts: In the chick trunk, they then let go of their neighbours, break through the basement membrane, and crawl away. In the mouse head, many leave before the folds have closed.
scenes.visual: Label: chick trunk. Gold cells release from the top of the closed tube one by one; inset shows contacts between neighbours letting go. Small note: mouse head, many leave before closure.
scenes.narration: In the chick trunk, they then let go of their neighbours, break through the basement membrane, and crawl away. In the mouse head, many leave before the folds have closed.

scenes.tts: This change, from a cell in a sheet to a free cell, is an epithelial to mesenchymal transition.
scenes.caption: This change, from a cell in a sheet to a free cell, is an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, or EMT.
scenes.narration: This change, from a cell in a sheet to a free cell, is an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, or EMT.

scenes.tts: What they become differs along the body.
scenes.visual: A side view of the embryo's body axis with five coloured levels: cranial, vagal, cardiac, trunk and sacral.
scenes.narration: What they become differs along the body.

scenes.tts: Cranial crest makes cartilage and bone of the face and much of the skull.
scenes.visual: A stream from the cranial level fans into the face; facial cartilage and bone light up.
scenes.narration: Cranial crest makes cartilage and bone of the face and much of the skull.

scenes.tts: Vagal and sacral crest make the neurons and glia of the gut wall.
scenes.visual: Streams from the neck and tail levels enter the gut wall; small gut ganglia appear.
scenes.narration: Vagal and sacral crest make the neurons and glia of the gut wall.

scenes.tts: Trunk crest makes sensory and sympathetic neurons, adrenal medulla, Schwann cells and melanocytes, the pigment cells.
scenes.visual: Trunk streams reach a dorsal root ganglion, a sympathetic ganglion, the adrenal gland, a nerve and the skin.
scenes.narration: Trunk crest makes sensory and sympathetic neurons, adrenal medulla, Schwann cells and melanocytes, the pigment cells.

scenes.tts: Here is the one idea to carry through. One border, many destinations.
scenes.narration: Here is the one idea to carry through. One border, many destinations.

scenes.tts: Where along the body a crest population starts biases what it can become.
scenes.visual: The card adds: the start biases the options.
scenes.narration: Where along the body a crest population starts biases what it can become.

scenes.tts: The signals on its route, and where it stops, help decide which fates appear.
scenes.visual: The card adds: route and stopping place help choose.
scenes.narration: The signals on its route, and where it stops, help decide which fates appear.

scenes.tts: This holds for populations. Some single cells are already biased before they leave.
scenes.visual: A small note under the card: populations, not every cell; some cells are biased early.
scenes.narration: This holds for populations. Some single cells are already biased before they leave.

scenes.tts: Many tissues share that start, and many need the same genes. So one failed gene can strike tissues that look unrelated.
scenes.visual: Lines run from the gold border to gut neurons, skin and inner ear.
scenes.narration: Many tissues share that start, and many need the same genes. So one failed gene can strike tissues that look unrelated.

scenes.tts: Predict. If gut neurons and pigment cells share a start, what could one broken gene do?
scenes.visual: The puzzle returns: the gut, the forelock and the ear, each with a question mark.
scenes.narration: Predict. If gut neurons and pigment cells share a start, what could one broken gene do?

scenes.tts: It could fail both lineages at once, if both need that gene. Chapter three names the genes.
scenes.visual: One gene icon wired to both enteric precursors and melanocytes; both dim together.
scenes.narration: It could fail both lineages at once, if both need that gene. Chapter three names the genes.

scenes.tts: The takeaway. The start biases the options, and the journey helps choose.
scenes.visual: Closing card: the start biases; the journey helps choose.
scenes.narration: The takeaway. The start biases the options, and the journey helps choose.
